paragraphs.heading: A star that pulses
paragraphs.text: A Cepheid variable is a star that pulsates: it swells and shrinks, and its temperature rises and falls along with its size. Its brightness changes on a steady, well-defined period, typically somewhere between 1 and 100 days. The name comes from Delta Cephei, in the constellation Cepheus, one of the early examples found.

paragraphs.heading: A cosmic measuring stick
paragraphs.text: What makes Cepheids so useful is that a Cepheid's luminosity is tightly linked to its pulsation period. Henrietta Swan Leavitt found this link in 1908 while studying thousands of variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds, and she published it in 1912. Time the pulses and you learn the star's true luminosity. Compare that with how bright it looks from Earth and you get its distance. The scale is calibrated with parallax distances to the closest Cepheids, such as Polaris and RS Puppis.

paragraphs.heading: How the pulsing works
paragraphs.text: Cepheids pulse through the κ–mechanism, which happens when a star's atmosphere becomes more opaque as it gets hotter instead of less. Helium is thought to be the main gas at work. Squeezing the outer layer heats its helium until it becomes doubly ionized, a form that is more opaque than singly ionized helium. Being opaque, it absorbs enough heat to expand; then it cools, turns singly ionized and transparent again, and keeps cooling until it collapses. The star is at its dimmest while the helium is doubly ionized.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the universe
paragraphs.text: In 1918 Harlow Shapley used Cepheids to put early limits on how big the Milky Way is, what shape it has, and where the Sun lies in it. In 1924 Edwin Hubble found the distance to Cepheids in the Andromeda Galaxy, then called the Andromeda Nebula, and showed they were not part of the Milky Way. That answered the Great Debate over whether our galaxy was the whole Universe or one galaxy among many. Later, Cepheid distances to several galaxies were combined with Vesto Slipher's measurements of how fast those galaxies move away, giving Hubble's law and showing that the Universe is expanding.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of Cepheid
paragraphs.text: In the 1940s Walter Baade recognized that Cepheids come in two separate populations. Classical Cepheids are younger and more massive, while type II Cepheids are older and fainter, by about 1.5 magnitudes on average. The two follow different period–luminosity relationships. Sorting them out doubled the distance to the Andromeda Galaxy and to the galaxies beyond it.

paragraphs.heading: Big, bright and yellow
paragraphs.text: Classical Cepheids hold 4 to 20 times the Sun's mass and shine up to 100,000 times more luminously. They are yellow bright giants and supergiants, and over one cycle their radius changes by millions of kilometers. Astronomers use them to find distances to galaxies in the Local Group and farther away, and as one way to pin down the Hubble constant. Closer to home, they have helped map the Milky Way's local spiral structure and the Sun's height above the galactic plane.
